pos: v. (preterite of slay: killed, put to death; rendering Hebrew harag, Greek anaireo)
etymology: Preterite of slay, from the Saxon slean, to strike or kill — the same root as slaughter. The strong past form slew has survived in English almost entirely because the Authorized Version carried it, and it retains a gravity that killed has lost.
biblical_def: Slew is the Authorized Version's past tense of slay, and it is used for deliberate killing rather than accidental death. It carries the first recorded human sin after Eden: “Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him” (Genesis 4:8) — and the verse withholds the word until the last clause, so that the sentence enacts the ambush it describes. From that point the word tracks the violence of the fallen world through Scripture, and it is applied both to lawful executions under the judicial law and to murders. Its gravest use is apostolic. Peter charges the nation at Jerusalem with the death of Christ in the plainest possible terms: “The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom ye slew and hanged on a tree” (Acts 5:30). The pronoun is second person and the verb is active; there is no softening. Yet the same sermons that press the charge offer pardon to the men charged, which is the pattern of apostolic preaching — full guilt named, full remission offered. The word appears too in the celebration of victory that ruined Saul: “Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands” (1 Samuel 18:7), where a song of praise becomes the seed of murderous envy in a king who could not bear comparison.
webster_summary: The preterite of slay — killed deliberately. It carries Cain's murder of Abel and Peter's charge to Jerusalem, whom ye slew and hanged on a tree.
webster_full: SLEW, pret. of slay. [Sax. slean, to strike, to kill.] Killed; put to death by violence.
2. Applied to the destruction of men in battle; as, he slew a thousand men.
3. Used of judicial execution under the law; as, the avenger of blood slew the murderer.
4. In Scripture, of the first murder; as, Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him, Gen. 4.
5. Of the crucifixion; as, whom ye slew and hanged on a tree, Acts 5.
corruption_summary: Modern English has retired slew to legend and headline, where it sounds heroic or quaint. In Scripture it is a heavy word for deliberate killing, and it is levelled at the reader as directly as at Cain.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The change is one of register rather than doctrine: slew now belongs to dragons and sports pages, and the drift toward the bloodless killed or the clinical terminated costs something real. Genesis 4:8 does not describe an incident; it describes a brother rising up. Our Lord traced murder back to the anger in the heart, and the Authorized Version's heavier verb keeps the act from being filed away as a category of crime rather than a fruit of a nature.

The principle to recover is the directness of Acts 5:30. Peter does not say that Jesus died, nor that circumstances converged; he says ye slew him, addressing men in the crowd, and he says it as the prelude to offering them forgiveness and the gift of the Holy Ghost. Preaching that cannot name guilt in the second person cannot offer pardon in the second person either, and a gospel that never says ye slew will never get round to saying be it known unto you therefore that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins.
roots_summary: Hebrew harag is to kill or slay, the verb used of Cain; nakah is to smite, often fatally. Greek anaireo is to take up and so to do away with, Luke's word for judicial killing, and apokteino is simply to kill.
roots_lines: Hebrew harag (H2026) — to kill, to slay; used of Cain's act against Abel.
Hebrew nakah (H5221) — to smite, to strike, often to death; the root behind smitten.
Hebrew ratsach (H7523) — to murder; the specific verb of the sixth commandment.
Greek anaireo (G337) — to take away, to make away with; Luke's term in Acts 5:30.
Greek apokteino (G615) — to kill outright; used of the killing of the prophets and of Christ.
usage: Of the first murder: Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him (Genesis 4:8).
Of the crucifixion charged directly to the hearers: whom ye slew and hanged on a tree (Acts 5:30).
Of the song that bred a king's envy: Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands (1 Samuel 18:7).
scriptures: And Cain talked with Abel his brother: and it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him.
The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom ye slew and hanged on a tree.
And the women answered one another as they played, and said, Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.
Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.

pos: v. (past participle of slay: killed, put to death; rendering Hebrew chalal, Greek sphazo)
etymology: Past participle of slay, from the Saxon slean. The Greek behind its most important New Testament use is sphazo, to slaughter as a sacrifice — the word for cutting a victim's throat at the altar, not for killing in general.
biblical_def: Slain is the participle, and it is the great word of the book of Revelation, where it becomes a permanent title. John turns to see the Lion of the tribe of Judah and beholds instead a Lamb as it had been slain, and heaven's song fastens on that: “Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength” (Revelation 5:12). The Greek verb is sacrificial, the altar word, so the slaying is not a defeat that was afterwards reversed but the very ground of the Lamb's worthiness — he is worthy because he was slain. The marks remain on the glorified body; the wounds are not erased but enthroned. Revelation gives the doctrine its eternal dimension in the phrase “the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world” (Revelation 13:8), which places the cross inside God's eternal purpose rather than treating it as a remedy improvised after the fall. The word also describes the church's own portion in this world, quoted by Paul from the Psalter: “for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter” (Psalm 44:22) — the flock shares the pattern of the Lamb, and Romans 8 answers that in all these things we are more than conquerors.
webster_summary: Past participle of slay. In Revelation it becomes the Lamb's permanent title — worthy is the Lamb that was slain — the Greek being the altar word for a sacrificial victim.
webster_full: SLAIN, pp. of slay. Killed; put to death by violence.
2. As a noun, those who have been killed; as, the slain of the LORD shall be many, Isa. 66.
3. Of a sacrificial victim, slaughtered at the altar.
4. In Scripture, of Christ; as, the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world, Rev. 13.
5. Of the church's afflictions; as, counted as sheep for the slaughter, Psa. 44, Rom. 8.
corruption_summary: A sanitised Christianity finds the slain Lamb primitive and prefers a cross that teaches or inspires. Revelation makes the slaying the ground of the Lamb's worthiness and keeps the wounds visible in glory.
corruption_paragraphs: The recurring objection to substitutionary atonement calls it barbaric — blood religion, a God requiring death. Nineteenth-century liberalism recast Calvary as moral example, and later writers have called penal substitution divine child abuse. Revelation 5:12 stands in the way of every such revision. Heaven's worship does not honour the Lamb despite the slaughter or in memory of a tragic misunderstanding; it names the slaying as the reason for the worthiness, and the whole company of the redeemed sings it.

There is also a sentimental error inside the church that hurries past the cross to the empty tomb, as though the wounds were an embarrassment now behind us. But the Lamb in the throne room appears as it had been slain, and Thomas was invited to the marks. The principle to recover is that Revelation 13:8 places the slaying in the eternal counsel of God: the cross is not God's reaction to a spoiled creation but the purpose to which creation itself was ordered, and the Lamb was slain from the foundation of the world.
roots_summary: Hebrew chalal is one pierced or fatally wounded, the standard term for the slain in battle. Greek sphazo is to slaughter sacrificially, the verb of Revelation, while thuo is to sacrifice and arnion is the little lamb of John's vision.
roots_lines: Hebrew chalal (H2491) — pierced, fatally wounded, slain; the word for battlefield dead.
Hebrew zabach (H2076) — to slaughter for sacrifice; the altar verb of the Levitical system.
Greek sphazo (G4969) — to slay as a victim, to cut the throat; used of the Lamb in Revelation 5.
Greek arnion (G721) — a little lamb; John's distinctive term for the slain and reigning Christ.
Greek thuo (G2380) — to sacrifice; Christ our passover is sacrificed for us, 1 Corinthians 5:7.
usage: Of the ground of the Lamb's worthiness: worthy is the Lamb that was slain (Revelation 5:12).
Of the cross within God's eternal purpose: the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world (Revelation 13:8).
Of the church's portion in this world: we are counted as sheep for the slaughter (Psalm 44:22).
scriptures: Saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing.
And all that dwell upon the earth shall worship him, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.
Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.
And the women answered one another as they played, and said, Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.

pos: v. (preterite and participle of seek; rendering Hebrew darash and baqash, Greek zeteo)
etymology: Preterite of seek, from the Saxon secan. Hebrew darash is to enquire of, to consult, and came to mean the diligent study of the law; baqash is to seek with desire, to search out. The English past tense preserves the sense of a search already made and answered.
biblical_def: Sought records seeking as an accomplished act, and Scripture is careful about what men seek and who seeks first. Of the believer it is the language of testimony: “I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears” (Psalm 34:4), and the Psalmist stakes his integrity on wholeness of pursuit, “With my whole heart have I sought thee: O let me not wander from thy commandments” (Psalm 119:10) — where even the man who has sought with his whole heart prays against wandering, which is honest about the residue of sin. But the decisive use reverses the direction. Isaiah records God saying, “I am sought of them that asked not for me; I am found of them that sought me not” (Isaiah 65:1) — a verse Paul applies to the calling of the Gentiles, and one of the clearest statements in the Old Testament that God takes the initiative in salvation. Men are found who were not looking. Ecclesiastes supplies the counterweight and diagnoses what unregenerate seeking actually pursues: “God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions” (Ecclesiastes 7:29). The faculty of seeking survived the fall; its direction did not.
webster_summary: Preterite of seek. Believers testify that they sought the LORD and were heard; but Isaiah 65:1 reverses the direction — I am found of them that sought me not — and grace is prior.
webster_full: SOUGHT, pret. and pp. of seek. [Sax. secan, to seek.] Went in search of; endeavored to find; solicited.
2. Asked for; requested; as, he sought counsel of the Lord.
3. Aimed at; endeavored to obtain; as, they sought his life.
4. Studied out; contrived; as, they have sought out many inventions, Eccl. 7.
5. In Scripture, I sought the Lord, and he heard me, Psa. 34; I am found of them that sought me not, Isa. 65.
corruption_summary: The spiritual search is now spoken of as the seeker's achievement, and church programmes are built round the seeker. Scripture says the natural man seeks out inventions, and that God is found of those who were not seeking him.
corruption_paragraphs: Seeker-centred ministry rests on an anthropology Scripture does not grant. Romans states flatly that there is none that seeketh after God, and Ecclesiastes 7:29 explains what the search faculty produces when left to itself — many inventions, the endless manufacture of religion. That is not a denial that men are religious; it is an account of why their religion never arrives. The seeking that finds God is itself the fruit of grace already at work, which is why Isaiah 65:1 can put the discovery before the search.

The correction must not be pressed into fatalism. Psalm 34:4 and Psalm 119:10 are genuine testimonies of genuine seeking, and Scripture everywhere commands men to seek the LORD while he may be found. Both are true because effectual calling does not bypass the will but renews it: God seeks first, and the man he has sought then seeks him, and seeks him with his whole heart. The principle to recover is the order. Where the order is reversed, assurance rests on the strength of one's own pursuit, which is a poor foundation on a bad day.
roots_summary: Hebrew darash is to enquire of or consult, later to study the law; baqash is to seek with desire. Greek zeteo is to seek and ekzeteo to seek out diligently, the word of Hebrews 11:6.
roots_lines: Hebrew darash (H1875) — to enquire, to consult, to seek diligently; the root of later Jewish midrash.
Hebrew baqash (H1245) — to seek, to search out, to desire; used of seeking God's face.
Greek zeteo (G2212) — to seek; seek ye first the kingdom of God.
Greek ekzeteo (G1567) — to seek out earnestly; God is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.
Greek epizeteo (G1934) — to seek after, to crave; used of what the Gentiles seek after.
usage: Of answered seeking: I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears (Psalm 34:4).
Of grace preceding the search: I am found of them that sought me not (Isaiah 65:1).
Of what fallen men actually seek: they have sought out many inventions (Ecclesiastes 7:29).
scriptures: I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears.
With my whole heart have I sought thee: O let me not wander from thy commandments.
I am sought of them that asked not for me; I am found of them that sought me not: I said, Behold me, behold me, unto a nation that was not called by my name.
Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions.

pos: v. (preterite and participle of flee; rendering Hebrew nus and barach, Greek pheugo)
etymology: Preterite of flee, from the Saxon fleon. Hebrew nus is to flee for refuge — the verb of the cities of refuge — while barach is to run away, to escape, the word used of Jonah's flight and of a bolt sliding through its rings.
biblical_def: Fled is used in Scripture for flight that is cowardice, for flight that is obedience, and for the flight of the created order before its Judge. Joseph's is the pattern of righteous flight: when his master's wife caught him by his garment, “he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out” (Genesis 39:12). Scripture never counsels a man to stand and reason with that temptation; the command is to flee fornication, and Joseph lost his coat and kept his integrity. The disciples show the other kind: “And they all forsook him, and fled” (Mark 14:50) — five words that indict the whole company and prepare for the restoration of Peter, so that the men who fled became the men who would not flee again under Nero. Jonah supplies the impossible flight: he “rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD” (Jonah 1:3), and the narrative spends four chapters demonstrating that there is no such destination. Finally the word describes the dissolution of the world at the judgment: John sees a great white throne, “from whose face the earth and the heaven fled away; and there was found no place for them” (Revelation 20:11). Creation itself cannot stand before that face.
webster_summary: Preterite of flee. Joseph fled temptation and lost his garment; the disciples fled their Lord; Jonah fled a presence he could not escape; and earth and heaven flee before the throne.
webster_full: FLED, pret. and pp. of flee. [Sax. fleon.] Ran away; escaped; departed in haste to avoid danger.
2. Withdrew; disappeared; vanished; as, the shadows fled.
3. To flee from, to shun; to avoid; as, flee youthful lusts.
4. In Scripture, of righteous flight; as, he left his garment, and fled, Gen. 39.
5. Of the dissolution of the world; as, the earth and the heaven fled away, Rev. 20.
corruption_summary: Flight is read as weakness — the counsel of an age that prizes confrontation and self-mastery. Scripture commands flight from certain sins as the only wise course, and reserves censure for fleeing one's duty and one's Lord.
corruption_paragraphs: Much popular teaching on temptation urges the believer to stand, resist, and master the desire, and Scripture does say resist the devil. But it says something different about particular sins: flee fornication, flee from idolatry, flee youthful lusts. Joseph did not rebuke his mistress or reason with her; he ran, and left evidence behind that would be used to imprison him. A man who will not run because running looks weak has already conceded the ground, and the modern conviction that maturity means being able to stay in the room is precisely what Genesis 39:12 contradicts.

The word's other uses supply the balance, so that flight is not commended indiscriminately. Mark 14:50 records desertion, and Jonah 1:3 records disobedience dressed as travel — and the LORD sent a wind after him. The principle to recover is discernment about direction. Fleeing temptation is obedience; fleeing duty, or the presence of God, only shortens the distance to the storm. And Revelation 20:11 sets the final term to all flight: from that throne earth and heaven find no place, and the only refuge left is the one Hebrews names, having fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us.
roots_summary: Hebrew nus is to flee for refuge, the verb of the cities of refuge; barach is to run away or escape. Greek pheugo is to flee, giving fugitive, and katapheugo is to flee down to a refuge.
roots_lines: Hebrew nus (H5127) — to flee, to escape to safety; used of the manslayer fleeing to the city of refuge.
Hebrew barach (H1272) — to run away, to bolt; used of Jonah's flight toward Tarshish.
Greek pheugo (G5343) — to flee; the imperative in flee fornication and flee from idolatry.
Greek katapheugo (G2703) — to flee for refuge; Hebrews 6:18, fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope.
Greek ekpheugo (G1628) — to escape out; how shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation.
usage: Of righteous flight from temptation: he left his garment in her hand, and fled (Genesis 39:12).
Of desertion: they all forsook him, and fled (Mark 14:50).
Of creation before the throne: from whose face the earth and the heaven fled away (Revelation 20:11).
scriptures: And she caught him by his garment, saying, Lie with me: and he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out.
And they all forsook him, and fled.

But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD.
And I saw a great white throne, and him that sat on it, from whose face the earth and the heaven fled away; and there was found no place for them.

pos: v. (preterite of arise: rose up, stood up, set out; rendering Hebrew qum, Greek anistemi)
etymology: Preterite of arise, from the Saxon arisan. Hebrew qum means to stand up and very often to begin acting — the Hebrew narrative idiom he arose and went marks decision, not merely posture — and Greek anistemi is the standard verb both for getting up and for resurrection.
biblical_def: Arose is one of the great hinge words of biblical narrative. In Hebrew idiom a man arises before he acts, so the word marks the moment resolve becomes motion. The prodigal's repentance turns on it: having said I will arise and go to my father, the text records that “he arose, and came to his father” (Luke 15:20), and the distance between resolution and arising is where most repentance dies. Deborah's song uses it of God raising up a deliverer in a collapsing nation: the villages ceased “until that I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel” (Judges 5:7). Mark uses it for the immediate evidence of Christ's authority: at his word the palsied man “immediately he arose, took up the bed, and went forth before them all” (Mark 2:12), the healing proving the forgiveness that had just been pronounced. And the word can mark flight as easily as obedience, for Jonah too “rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD” (Jonah 1:3) — the same decisive verb, aimed the wrong way. Its greatest weight is that the Greek behind it, anistemi, is the resurrection verb; the ordinary rising of a man from his bed and the rising of the dead are named alike.
webster_summary: Preterite of arise — rose up, and in Hebrew idiom, set about acting. The prodigal arose and came to his father; and the Greek behind it is the New Testament's resurrection verb.
webster_full: AROSE, pret. of arise. [Sax. arisan.] Rose up; got up from a sitting, lying or kneeling posture.
2. Proceeded; issued; sprang; as, a dispute arose among them.
3. Began to act; set out; as, he arose and went on his journey.
4. Was raised up by God for a purpose; as, until that I Deborah arose, Judges 5.
5. In Scripture, of the prodigal; as, he arose, and came to his father, Luke 15.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word's force is lost by familiarity rather than by attack: a narrative hinge is read as scene-setting, and the decisive step it marks goes unnoticed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What has weakened is attention. Readers pass over and he arose as stage direction, when in Hebrew narrative it is the point at which intention becomes action. Luke 15 makes the structure visible by giving the sentence twice: first the prodigal says in the far country, I will arise and go to my father, and then the narrative says he arose and came. The whole parable turns in that gap, and the gap is where a great many men live — convinced, resolved, and still in the far country.

The principle to recover is that Scripture regularly makes repentance a matter of rising and moving rather than of feeling. Mark 2:12 shows the same logic in the physical order: Christ pronounces forgiveness, which cannot be seen, and then commands a rising that can, so that the visible arising authenticates the invisible pardon. And because anistemi is also the resurrection verb, every such rising in the Gospels is a small rehearsal of the last one, when all that are in the graves shall hear his voice and shall come forth.
roots_summary: Hebrew qum is to stand up, to arise, and so to set about a thing; it is also the verb of covenant establishment. Greek anistemi is to stand up or raise up, the ordinary resurrection verb, and egeiro is to awaken or raise.
roots_lines: Hebrew qum (H6965) — to arise, to stand, to be established; the narrative hinge verb.
Hebrew talitha cumi — damsel, arise; the Aramaic imperative our Lord spoke over Jairus' daughter.
Greek anistemi (G450) — to stand up, to rise; used of rising from sleep and of resurrection alike.
Greek egeiro (G1453) — to awaken, to raise up; he is not here: for he is risen.
Greek anastasis (G386) — a standing up again, resurrection; the noun formed from anistemi.
usage: Of repentance becoming motion: he arose, and came to his father (Luke 15:20).
Of a deliverer raised up in a failing nation: until that I Deborah arose (Judges 5:7).
Of healing that authenticates pardon: immediately he arose, took up the bed, and went forth (Mark 2:12).
scriptures: And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
The inhabitants of the villages ceased, they ceased in Israel, until that I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel.
And immediately he arose, took up the bed, and went forth before them all; insomuch that they were all amazed, and glorified God, saying, We never saw it on this fashion.

But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD.

pos: v. (preterite of dwell: abode, resided; rendering Hebrew yashab and shakan, Greek skenoo and meno)
etymology: Preterite of dwell, from the Saxon dwellan, which first meant to delay or tarry and only later to reside — dwelling is tarrying that has become permanent. Hebrew shakan is to settle down, the root of mishkan, the tabernacle, and of the later term shekinah.
biblical_def: Dwelt is a quiet word carrying one of the highest doctrines in Scripture. John chooses it for the incarnation, and his Greek is precise: “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). The verb is skenoo, to pitch a tent, deliberately recalling the tabernacle in the wilderness where the glory settled between the cherubim; the eternal Word did not visit humanity but tented in it, and the glory once veiled behind curtains was now veiled in flesh. The Old Testament pattern behind this is the patriarchal life of faith, which Hebrews summarises: Abraham “sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob” (Hebrews 11:9) — men who owned the promise and pitched tents, because they looked for a city with foundations. Luke closes Acts with the same word used of unglamorous faithfulness: “And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him” (Acts 28:30), an apostle under guard, still preaching, the book ending without a verdict because the gospel's progress never depended on one.
webster_summary: Preterite of dwell — abode, resided. John's word for the incarnation is skenoo, to pitch a tent: the Word was made flesh and tabernacled among us.
webster_full: DWELT, pret. and pp. of dwell. [Sax. dwellan, to tarry.] Abode; resided; inhabited; continued in a place.
2. To remain; to continue; to be fixed in attention; as, to dwell upon a subject.
3. Of tent-dwelling; as, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, Heb. 11.
4. In Scripture, of the incarnation; the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, John 1.
5. Of the indwelling of God; as, in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily, Col. 2.
corruption_summary: The incarnation is often reduced to God visiting or appearing — a temporary manifestation. John's verb says the Word pitched his tent among us, took real flesh, and did not lay it down at the ascension.
corruption_paragraphs: Every ancient error about Christ's person can be described as a refusal of this verb. Docetism said he only seemed to have flesh; Apollinarianism gave him a body without a human mind; Nestorianism held the two natures so far apart that no single person truly dwelt among us; Eutychianism blended them into a third thing that is neither God nor man. Chalcedon answered them all with one Person in two natures, without confusion, change, division, or separation — which is simply John 1:14 defended. The modern versions of the error are vaguer but the same: Christ as an inspired man, or as God appearing in human costume.

The principle to recover is the permanence of the dwelling. Christ did not shed his humanity when he ascended; he sits at the Father's right hand as the God-man and will return in the body in which he suffered. That is why Hebrews can make him a High Priest touched with the feeling of our infirmities, and why the patriarchs' tent-dwelling in Hebrews 11:9 is more than local colour — the men who dwelt in tents looked for a city, and the Word who tented among us is preparing it.
roots_summary: Hebrew yashab is to sit or remain, the ordinary word for residing, while shakan is to settle or tabernacle, giving mishkan and shekinah. Greek skenoo is to pitch a tent and meno is to abide or remain.
roots_lines: Hebrew yashab (H3427) — to sit, to remain, to inhabit; the common verb for dwelling in a place.
Hebrew shakan (H7931) — to settle down, to tabernacle; used of the glory dwelling between the cherubim.
Hebrew mishkan (H4908) — tabernacle, dwelling place; the tent God commanded Moses to raise.
Greek skenoo (G4637) — to pitch a tent, to tabernacle; John's verb for the incarnation.
Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, to remain; abide in me, and I in you.
usage: Of the incarnation: the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us (John 1:14).
Of patriarchal faith holding the promise in tents: dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob (Hebrews 11:9).
Of unglamorous apostolic faithfulness: Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house (Acts 28:30).
scriptures: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise:
And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him,
From the place of his habitation he looketh upon all the inhabitants of the earth.

pos: v. (preterite of weep: shed tears, lamented; rendering Hebrew bakah, Greek klaio and dakruo)
etymology: Preterite of weep, from the Saxon wepan, which is related to wop, a cry — weeping in the older English is audible, not merely wet. Hebrew bakah is likewise a loud lamentation, and the Greek distinguishes klaio, to wail aloud, from dakruo, to shed tears quietly.
biblical_def: Wept guards the church against two errors at once, because the Son of God is its subject in the shortest verse of the Bible: “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). He weeps at the grave of Lazarus knowing that he will raise him within the hour, which forbids the notion that grief is unbelief; sorrow at death is not a failure of faith but the right response of a man to an enemy. The Greek there is dakruo, a quiet shedding of tears. A different word is used over the city: “when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it” (Luke 19:41), and this is klaio, the loud wailing of formal lament — our Lord audibly grieving over Jerusalem's coming judgment, days before the same city killed him. Peter's tears are the pattern of true repentance as distinct from remorse: remembering the word of Jesus, he “went out, and wept bitterly” (Matthew 26:75), and unlike Judas he came back. And the exiles teach the church how to sing in a strange land: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion” (Psalm 137:1). Scripture makes room for tears and appoints an end to them — God shall wipe away all tears.
webster_summary: Preterite of weep. Christ wept at a grave he was about to open and wailed aloud over a city that would kill him; Peter wept bitterly and was restored. Grief is not unbelief.
webster_full: WEPT, pret. and pp. of weep. [Sax. wepan, to cry out.] Shed tears; lamented; mourned audibly.
2. To lament; to bewail; as, to weep over one's sins.
3. To shed moisture, as a tree or a wound — a figurative use.
4. In Scripture, of Christ; as, Jesus wept, John 11; he beheld the city, and wept over it, Luke 19.
5. Of repentance; as, Peter went out and wept bitterly, Matt. 26.
corruption_summary: Grief is handled either as a problem to be processed or as a weakness unbecoming to faith. Scripture shows the Son of God weeping at a grave he was about to open, and appoints a day when the tears are wiped away.
corruption_paragraphs: One error belongs to a triumphalist piety that treats tears as evidence of insufficient faith, so that mourners are hurried toward rejoicing and told not to grieve. Paul does not say that: he says sorrow not, even as others which have no hope, which regulates grief rather than forbidding it. John 11:35 settles the matter, since Christ wept in full knowledge of the resurrection he was minutes from performing. If certainty about the outcome does not dry the tears of the Son of God, it need not dry ours.

The other error is the therapeutic reframing that makes grief a process with stages to be completed and a self to be restored. Scripture treats tears as testimony rather than as a task — the Psalmist asks God to put his tears in a bottle — and locates their end not in successful adjustment but in a promise: God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes. The principle to recover is that Christian mourning is neither suppressed nor endless. Peter's bitter weeping in Matthew 26:75 is the model of the sorrow that works repentance to salvation, not to be repented of, and it ended on a beach in Galilee with a threefold restoration.
roots_summary: Hebrew bakah is to weep aloud, giving Bochim, the place of weepers. Greek distinguishes klaio, to wail audibly, from dakruo, to shed tears — the latter used only of Christ at Lazarus' tomb.
roots_lines: Hebrew bakah (H1058) — to weep, to lament audibly; used of Israel at Bochim and of Hannah at Shiloh.
Hebrew dimah (H1832) — tears; the Psalmist prays that God would put his tears into his bottle.
Greek klaio (G2799) — to wail aloud, to lament; the word for Christ's weeping over Jerusalem.
Greek dakruo (G1145) — to shed tears silently; used only once, of Jesus at the grave of Lazarus.
Greek pentheo (G3996) — to mourn; blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted.
usage: Of Christ at a grave he was about to open: Jesus wept (John 11:35).
Of audible lament over a city under judgment: he beheld the city, and wept over it (Luke 19:41).
Of repentance distinguished from remorse: Peter went out, and wept bitterly (Matthew 26:75).
scriptures: And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it,
And Peter remembered the word of Jesus, which said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And he went out, and wept bitterly.
By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion.

pos: v. (preterite of draw: pulled, drew out, approached; rendering Hebrew mashah and nagash, Greek helko and eggizo)
etymology: Preterite of draw, from the Saxon dragan, to pull or drag. Hebrew mashah is to draw out of water, and Pharaoh's daughter names Moses from it; nagash is to draw near, especially to approach God, and it is the priestly word for approach.
biblical_def: Drew covers pulling, drawing out, and drawing near, and Scripture uses all three theologically. The drawing out of water names the deliverer: Pharaoh's daughter “called his name Moses: and she said, Because I drew him out of the water” (Exodus 2:10) — a name that will describe his life's work, since the man drawn out of the Nile draws a nation out of the sea. The drawing of a sword marks the failure of the flesh to defend the kingdom: in Gethsemane one of them “stretched out his hand, and drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest” (Matthew 26:51), and our Lord healed the wound and told him to put it up, for they that take the sword shall perish with the sword. The most tender use is the drawing near of the risen Christ to men who did not know him: while the two on the Emmaus road “communed together and reasoned, Jesus himself drew near, and went with them” (Luke 24:15). He does not begin with the disclosure but with the company, and expounds the Scriptures before he breaks the bread. The verb also carries the doctrine of effectual calling, for no man can come to Christ except the Father draw him.
webster_summary: Preterite of draw — pulled, drew out, drew near. Moses was drawn out of the water, Peter drew a sword and was rebuked, and the risen Christ drew near to men who did not know him.
webster_full: DREW, pret. of draw. [Sax. dragan, to pull.] Pulled; hauled; dragged along.
2. Pulled out; extracted; as, he drew his sword; she drew water from the well.
3. Attracted; allured; as, the multitude was drawn after him.
4. Approached; came near; as, the time drew nigh.
5. In Scripture, of effectual calling; no man can come to me, except the Father draw him, John 6.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The pressure is doctrinal rather than lexical: the drawing of John 6:44 is commonly softened into a general influence that men may finally refuse.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word's ordinary senses are stable. What is contested is one text, and the contest matters. In John 6:44 our Lord says no man can come to him except the Father draw him, and the verb helko is the word used of drawing a net full of fishes to shore and of Paul and Silas being dragged into the marketplace. It is not persuasion offered and possibly declined; and the same verse ends by promising that everyone so drawn will be raised up at the last day, which makes the drawing effectual by definition, since the group drawn and the group raised are one group.

The principle to recover is that this doctrine is a comfort rather than a threat, and Luke 24:15 shows why. The two on the Emmaus road were not seeking a risen Christ; they were leaving Jerusalem disappointed, saying they had trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel. He drew near to them. Effectual calling looks like that from the inside — not coercion, but a companion on the road who opens the Scriptures until the heart burns.
roots_summary: Hebrew mashah is to draw out of water, the root of the name Moses; nagash is to draw near, the priestly approach word. Greek helko is to drag or draw with force, and eggizo is to come near.
roots_lines: Hebrew mashah (H4871) — to draw out of water; the root of the name Moses in Exodus 2:10.
Hebrew nagash (H5066) — to draw near, to approach; used of priestly approach to the altar.
Hebrew mashak (H4900) — to draw, to drag; with lovingkindness have I drawn thee, Jeremiah 31:3.
Greek helko (G1670) — to draw, to drag; the verb of John 6:44 and of hauling in a full net.
Greek eggizo (G1448) — to draw near; draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you.
usage: Of the deliverer drawn from the water: because I drew him out of the water (Exodus 2:10).
Of the flesh defending the kingdom by force: drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest (Matthew 26:51).
Of the risen Christ approaching the discouraged: Jesus himself drew near, and went with them (Luke 24:15).
scriptures: And the child grew, and she brought him unto Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. And she called his name Moses: and she said, Because I drew him out of the water. Moses: that is, Drawn out
And, behold, one of them which were with Jesus stretched out his hand, and drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest's, and smote off his ear.
And it came to pass, that, while they communed together and reasoned, Jesus himself drew near, and went with them.
I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears.

pos: v. (past participle of smite: struck, afflicted; rendering Hebrew nakah, Greek patasso)
etymology: Past participle of smite, from the Saxon smitan, to strike. The Hebrew nakah covers everything from a blow of the hand to a plague sent from heaven, and its passive participle raises the question every sufferer asks — smitten by whom?
biblical_def: Smitten is the participle of being struck, and Scripture uses it above all of the Servant, where it exposes a fatal misreading and then corrects it. Isaiah writes: “Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted” (Isaiah 53:4). The onlookers were not wrong that he was smitten of God — the next verses say the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all — they were wrong about why. They assumed he was suffering for his own sin, as Job's friends assumed of Job, and that assumption is the oldest error in the theology of suffering. He was wounded for our transgressions, and the chastisement of our peace was upon him. The word also describes the believer's inner affliction with unusual honesty: “My heart is smitten, and withered like grass; so that I forget to eat my bread” (Psalm 102:4) — a description of grief so heavy that appetite fails, preserved in the Psalter as a prayer rather than edited out. Scripture does not present the life of faith as immune from being smitten, and it locates the meaning of the blow in God's hand rather than in the sufferer's guilt.
webster_summary: Past participle of smite — struck, afflicted. Isaiah's Servant was smitten of God, but for our transgressions and not his own; and the Psalter records hearts smitten and withered like grass.
webster_full: SMITTEN, pp. of smite. [Sax. smitan, to strike.] Struck; beaten; killed.
2. Afflicted; visited with judgment or with disease; as, smitten with a plague.
3. Affected with strong feeling; as, the heart is smitten.
4. Blasted; withered; as, the corn was smitten with blasting, Amos 4.
5. In Scripture, of the Servant; as, we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted, Isa. 53.
corruption_summary: Suffering is read as a verdict on the sufferer — the oldest error, and the one Job's friends made. Isaiah 53 shows the perfectly innocent One smitten of God, which severs the link between affliction and personal guilt.
corruption_paragraphs: The retribution reflex is universal and persistent: the sick man must have sinned, the bankrupt must have been foolish, the bereaved must have lacked faith. The disciples brought it to Christ at the man born blind — who did sin, this man, or his parents? — and he answered that neither had. Isaiah 53:4 records the same reflex operating at Calvary, where onlookers esteemed the Servant smitten of God and drew the obvious conclusion about his character. They were watching the atonement and reading it as a judgment on the victim's own record.

There is a modern variant in prosperity teaching, which simply runs the logic forwards: if the righteous are not smitten, then a man who is smitten must be deficient in faith or in giving. It is Job's comforters with a microphone, and it leaves the afflicted believer doubly burdened. The principle to recover is that Scripture assigns affliction to God's hand without assigning it to the sufferer's guilt. Psalm 102:4 prays honestly out of a smitten heart, and Isaiah 53 shows the only man who never deserved a blow taking every blow that we did.
roots_summary: Hebrew nakah is to strike, from a slap to a plague, and its passive participle is the word in Isaiah 53:4; maggephah is a stroke or plague. Greek patasso is to strike, used in I will smite the shepherd.
roots_lines: Hebrew nakah (H5221) — to smite, to strike, to afflict; used of blows, of plagues, and of the Servant.
Hebrew maggephah (H4046) — a stroke, a plague; the smiting sent among Israel.
Hebrew chalah (H2470) — to be weak or sick; the condition of one smitten with disease.
Greek patasso (G3960) — to strike, to smite; I will smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.
Greek mastigoo (G3146) — to scourge; whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son.
usage: Of the Servant misread by onlookers: we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted (Isaiah 53:4).
Of grief that takes away appetite: my heart is smitten, and withered like grass (Psalm 102:4).
Of a nation under judgment, as when Israel was smitten before her enemies for sin in the camp.
scriptures: Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.
My heart is smitten, and withered like grass; so that I forget to eat my bread.
Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.
And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it,

pos: v. (preterite of beseech: entreated earnestly; rendering Hebrew chanan, Greek parakaleo and deomai)
etymology: Preterite of beseech, from the intensive prefix be- and the Saxon secan, to seek — a thorough seeking, seeking with urgency. Greek parakaleo is to call alongside, the verb from which the Comforter takes his title, and deomai is to beg out of need.
biblical_def: Besought is earnest entreaty in the past tense, and Scripture uses it with a fine sense of who is begging whom. Paul's use is the best known: of his thorn in the flesh he says, “For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me” (2 Corinthians 12:8). Three times, and the answer was no — my grace is sufficient for thee — which makes this verse one of Scripture's plainest teachings on unanswered prayer: the request was refused and the petitioner was given something better than the request. Remarkably, devils also beseech: “So the devils besought him, saying, If thou cast us out, suffer us to go away into the herd of swine” (Matthew 8:31), and they are heard, which shows that being granted a petition is no evidence of standing with God. The healed Gadarene then “besought him that he might be with him” (Luke 8:38) — a good request, and denied; he is sent home to tell his friends instead. And Joseph's brothers remember, twenty years too late, the entreaty they refused: “We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear” (Genesis 42:21). Scripture places these together without comment, and the arrangement teaches.
webster_summary: Preterite of beseech — entreated earnestly. Paul besought the Lord thrice and was refused with something better; devils besought and were heard; and Joseph's brothers remembered too late the brother they would not hear.
webster_full: BESOUGHT, pret. and pp. of beseech. [be and Sax. secan, to seek.] Entreated; supplicated; implored; asked with urgency.
2. Begged earnestly for a favor; as, he besought him to depart out of their coasts.
3. Applied to prayer to God; as, I besought the Lord thrice, 2 Cor. 12.
4. Of one pleading for his life or liberty; as, when he besought us, and we would not hear, Gen. 42.
5. Sometimes used of an entreaty granted to the unworthy; as, the devils besought him, Matt. 8.
corruption_summary: Prayer is widely measured by results, so an unanswered request reads as failed faith or a defective God. Paul besought the Lord three times, was told no, and called the refusal grace.
corruption_paragraphs: The teaching that persistent, believing prayer secures the thing asked runs directly into 2 Corinthians 12:8. Paul was an apostle, his request was reasonable, and he made it three times — the same threefold pattern as our Lord in Gethsemane, whose cup also did not pass. The answer he received was not the thorn's removal but a promise: my grace is sufficient for thee, for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Any doctrine of prayer that cannot accommodate a refused apostle has left the New Testament behind.

Matthew 8:31 supplies the sharper edge, and it is rarely preached. The devils besought Christ and their petition was granted; the healed man in Luke 8:38 besought him and was refused. Getting what one asks for is therefore no measure of favour, and being refused is no measure of disfavour. The principle to recover is that prayer is submission to a wise Father rather than leverage upon him, and that the best answers are often the ones that decline the request. Joseph's brothers show the other side of the word: an entreaty ignored does not go away, and conscience produced their confession twenty years later in a foreign court.
roots_summary: Hebrew chanan in the reflexive stem is to implore favour, and tachanun is supplication. Greek parakaleo is to call alongside, to entreat or comfort, and deomai is to beg from need, the root of deesis, supplication.
roots_lines: Hebrew chanan (H2603) — in the reflexive, to implore favour, to make supplication.
Hebrew tachanun (H8469) — supplication, earnest entreaty; the poor useth intreaties, Proverbs 18:23.
Greek parakaleo (G3870) — to call alongside, to beseech, to comfort; the root of Paraclete.
Greek deomai (G1189) — to beg, to make request out of need; used of Paul's prayers for his brethren.
Greek deesis (G1162) — supplication; joined to prayer and thanksgiving in Philippians 4:6.
usage: Of prayer refused and answered with grace: I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me (2 Corinthians 12:8).
Of a petition granted to the unworthy: the devils besought him… suffer us to go away into the herd of swine (Matthew 8:31).
Of an entreaty ignored and remembered: when he besought us, and we would not hear (Genesis 42:21).
scriptures: For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me.
So the devils besought him, saying, If thou cast us out, suffer us to go away into the herd of swine.
And they said one to another, We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear; therefore is this distress come upon us.
Now the man out of whom the devils were departed besought him that he might be with him: but Jesus sent him away, saying,
